tldr: AUTOPATCH is a context-aware framework combining control flow graph (CFG) analysis and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to enable LLMs to generate optimized C++ code, achieving a 7.3% runtime improvement over GPT-4o.
contributions: Formalizing human programmer optimization strategies through CFG-based analysis
A unified approach integrating CFG diff analysis with RAG for context-aware code optimization
An automated in-context prompting pipeline that generates optimized code guided by structural insights and historical examples
methods: The framework analyzes Control Flow Graph (CFG) differences between unoptimized and optimized code pairs from the IBM Project CodeNet dataset, extracting structural changes (added/removed blocks), flow adjustments, and statement-level modifications. These CFG diffs are stored as embeddings alongside retrieved historical optimization examples in a vector database. The LLM (GPT-4o) is prompted with CFG difference analysis, optimization rationales, and exactly one top-ranked retrieved example to generate optimized patches for target C++ programs. Experiments used 1,000 code pairs for the vector database and 200 for testing, with embeddings generated by CodeBERT.
results: AUTOPATCH achieves a 7.3% improvement in execution time over zero-shot GPT-4o generation (0.3815s vs 0.4115s). Lexical similarity improved over baselines: Line Overlap +4.41%, Edit Distance Similarity +13.52%, Token Overlap +9.91%. AUTOPATCH showed the lowest average execution times across code refactoring, memory optimization, algorithmic simplification, and loop optimization categories. Naive generation was 27.3% slower than zero-shot (0.5238s vs 0.4115s). The test set contained 942 labeled optimization instances across five types.
limitations: The dataset is limited to C++ programs from IBM Project CodeNet, not representing full real-world codebase diversity or other languages. Only one retrieved example is used, limiting pattern variety. Code readability and maintainability may be affected by transformations like loop unrolling or branch merging. Execution time and lexical similarity metrics do not cover scalability or project-specific constraints. Some optimizations depend on hardware features or compiler behaviors outside the study's scope.
